nodes.label: Conflict rate is the deciding variable
nodes.rationale: The question is not which is better but how often two people collide on the same row. Order-of-magnitude guidance: under 1% optimistic comfortably; 1-10% optimistic with bounded retries and jittered backoff; over 10% pessimistic, or redesign so the hot row stops being hot. Naming the deciding variable is what an interviewer listens for; 'optimistic, always' loses.

nodes.label: The optimistic/pessimistic crossover point
nodes.rationale: At low contention optimistic wins easily — lock-free throughput, almost nothing conflicts. At high contention pessimistic wins because optimistic's retries multiply work while throughput stays flat. Where the crossover sits depends on transaction length and conflict rate, so measure rather than guess.

nodes.label: The cheapest concurrency control is needing none
nodes.rationale: If the whole operation fits in one SQL statement — UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 40 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 40 — the database does read-decide-write atomically and there is no gap to coordinate. Reach for this first; tokens and locks are for logic that does not fit.

nodes.label: Redesigning so the hot row stops being hot
nodes.rationale: Four moves that remove the contention rather than manage it: shard the counter across N rows summed on read, queue the writes and apply them serially, event-source by appending immutable events that cannot conflict, and batch many changes into one transaction.

nodes.label: Both strategies look identical in testing
nodes.rationale: With one user there are no conflicts, so optimistic never retries and pessimistic never waits. The difference appears only under concurrency, which is exactly when experimenting is hardest. This is why the lab forces the race and why forceRace:false exists — to show how rarely the problem surfaces by chance, and therefore how easily it reaches production.

hyperedges.label: Two correct strategies paying in different currencies
